runs.t: Residual Compensation of a Phenomenological Dynamic Asymmetric Ground-Effect Disturbance for UAV Landing on Moving Platforms: A Simulation Study of State-Space Safety Gating
Ravi Deo, Arjun Saharawat, Yash Bhadauria, Dharmendar Kumar and Ketan Anand
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
Sharda University, Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh, India

—Landing a multirotor on a laterally moving platform introduces near-ground disturbances that symmetric ground-effect corrections do not represent. We propose a phenomenological dynamic asymmetric ground-effect (DAGE) disturbance model with hypothesized airspeed-dependent and platform-slip-dependent terms, and train a residual controller to compensate it while a cascaded PID controller retains baseline authority. The study is deliberately conducted in a reduced-order simulation so that each element can be isolated and reproduced. Over 500 randomized Monte Carlo trials per condition, against proportional–derivative, tuned PID, and vertical-channel disturbance-observer baselines, the residual controller improves touchdown-envelope success from 80.8% to 100% at 3.0 m s
and from 3.6% to 96.2% at 5.0 m s

, 25% beyond the training-speed range. It retains a substantial advantage under a separately parameterized disturbance field, but degrades when speed extrapolation and model mismatch combine. A state-space distance gate meant to limit residual authority outside the training distribution is largely inactive at its calibrated threshold and hurts performance when tightened, indicating that state-space distance can be poorly aligned with residual-prediction reliability in closed loop. The results support residual compensation as a promising simulation-level approach, while the disturbance’s aerodynamic origin and transfer to physical UAVs remain open.
—UAV landing, moving platform, ground effect, residual learning, disturbance rejection, out-of-distribution detection, nonlinear control

Landing a multirotor on a laterally moving platform requires regulating position, velocity, attitude, and descent rate close to a surface, where rotor–surface interactions modify the forces and moments on the vehicle. Classical ground-effect models treat this mainly as a near-surface thrust increase [4] and do not specify the disturbance produced when vehicle and platform translate together. We therefore introduce a
model with two hypothesized contributions, one dependent on vehicle lateral airspeed and one on vehicle–platform lateral slip, and call the combined modeled disturbance

(DAGE), a name for our model rather than an established aerodynamic phenomenon. Since matching the platform velocity can remove the slip term while airspeed remains, good platform-velocity tracking does not by itself imply zero disturbance.

Model predictive control [3] depends on accurate near-ground dynamics, and end-to-end reinforcement learning offers no guarantees outside the training distribution without additional verification [10]. Residual learning keeps a nominal controller and learns only a correction around it [6]–[9]. Our contribution is as much methodological as architectural: residual-control results are easy to overstate in two ways, and we structure the evaluation to close both.

A PD comparison can exaggerate the benefit of residual learning when the disturbance has a sustained component, so we benchmark against a tuned PID cascade and a vertical-channel disturbance observer [11], [12] (Section VII-A).

Training and testing on the same disturbance family says little about robustness, so we also test a disturbance field with changed gains, length scales, altitude decay exponents, and mechanism weighting.
Third, we report a negative result: a state-distance residual-authority gate calibrated at the 99th percentile of in-distribution distance stays near full authority (
) even 50% beyond the training speed range, and tightening it reduces performance. We examine the distributional overlap behind this and a possible closed-loop self-masking effect.
A. Classical flight control and moving-platform landing
Cascaded PID remains the workhorse of multirotor control for its simplicity and predictable tuning [1], and geometric control on

(3) [2] avoids Euler-angle singularities in most modern attitude loops. Model predictive control suits moving-platform interception because it handles state and actuator constraints over a horizon [3], but relies on an accurate near-ground disturbance model.
B. Ground effect and the present disturbance model
The classical result is Cheeseman and Bennett’s momentum-theory correction for a rotor in forward flight near a surface [4]. Sanchez-Cuevas
[5] characterize multirotor ground effect experimentally and show that it matters near the surface; Yang
[14] model ground-effect-induced leveling torque and validate compensation in hardware; and Li
[15] study proximity effects on hovering multirotors. None of these establishes the moving-platform roll disturbance proposed here.

The closest work is Neural Lander [6], which adds a learned near-ground aerodynamic residual to a nonlinear tracking controller, with a spectral-normalization Lipschitz bound for stability, validated in real flight; Neural-Fly [7] extends this to online adaptation under wind, and residual policy learning [8], [9] frames the general idea. We claim no novelty for this pattern; what differs is the disturbance model and the information constraint, since platform velocity is unobserved and must be inferred from state and control history.
D. Classical alternatives and residual-authority gating

Disturbance-observer-based control and active disturbance rejection [11], [12] are classical tools for unmodeled additive disturbances; we include a vertical-channel DOB as a reference. Peng and Xia [13] place a deep network in the force and torque loop of a moving-platform landing controller with a stability analysis establishing uniformly ultimately bounded tracking error. Danesh
[16] consider uncertainty-aware policy adaptation under distribution shift, motivating our comparison of a state-distance gate with more direct uncertainty measures.

A. How much of the result is the baseline

, PD places 2.4% of landings inside the envelope versus 80.8% for PID, with larger RMS roll and lateral mismatch, consistent with the steady-state error a PD loop retains under a sustained disturbance (the gap’s size is specific to our gains and model). A PD-referenced result (2.4% → 100%) would conflate the learned correction with added integral action, so all comparisons below use PID (80.8% → 100%).
The vertical-channel DOB does not help in this configuration. At 3.0 m s
, PID+DOB lowers envelope success from 80.8% to 63.2% and raises RMS roll by 25% (paired difference +0.0073 rad, 95% CI [+0.0072, +0.0074],
). The observer acts only on the vertical channel, whereas the dominant DAGE term acts through roll; its higher impact speed (0.404 versus 0.335 m s
) is consistent with added vertical-command variation. A rotational or multivariable DOB was not evaluated, so this does not show DOB control to be inferior in general.

The network (24 → 64 → 64 → 32 → 2) has 7,906 parameters and needs 7,744 multiply–accumulate operations (15,488 FLOPs) per pass. Lacking STM32H7 hardware, we use published throughput: Garofalo
on GAP-8, 7.45× an STM32H7 running CMSIS-NN [22], implying about 0.143 GMAC s

and roughly 54 µs per pass, well inside the 10,000 µs budget of a 100 Hz loop. This is only an order-of-magnitude estimate: the cited figure is for an INT8 convolutional network, not float32 dense layers, excludes runtime overheads, and was not measured on the target.

Rotor aerodynamics, motor models, actuator saturation, platform geometry, and six-degree-of-freedom airframe dynamics are omitted, so aerodynamic validity and real-flight performance are not established.

Equations (6)–(7) are not derived from blade-element momentum theory, validated against CFD, or fitted to flight data. The mismatch study shows robustness within the chosen family, not that its structure or physical interpretation is correct.

Predictive utility from a 40 ms history does not establish observability or identifiability of platform motion; a history-length ablation and comparisons with explicit lateral- and platform-velocity measurements are needed.

We introduced a phenomenological DAGE disturbance model for UAV landing on a laterally translating platform and evaluated residual compensation for it in reduced-order simulation. The residual controller substantially improves touchdown quality over PID, including beyond the training speed range, and keeps a substantial advantage under model mismatch, although it degrades when mismatch and speed extrapolation combine; the state-distance gate provides little benefit, consistent with self-masking specific to this detector and architecture. Future work should use a higher-fidelity simulator with rotor and motor dynamics, compare the disturbance against CFD or measured force and torque data, vary the history length, and test uncertainty-aware gating under controlled distribution shift.
